name: Green Maw

facts.text: Level 65, 10,000 health, in the Cursed Forest. When it dies it splits into nine Parts of Green Maw in three sizes (levels about 58-60, 53-55 and 50).

In Cath Maige Tuired, the Fomorians fill a pit with porridge of milk, meal, fat, goats, sheep and swine and threaten the Dagda with death unless he eats it all; he eats it with a ladle big enough for a man and a woman to lie in, scrapes the bottom with his finger and sleeps.
facts.source: Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Mag Tuired)

facts.text: Living Server lore: the Ardee grandmothers setting the Dagda's porridge against the Green Maw, and the children's counting song at the pool.

story:
The pools of the Cursed Forest went bad with the rest of the wood, and in one of them a hunger grew. Green Maw is only a mouth: a mass of green slime as big as a cart with teeth around the edge, that eats what falls in and what wanders by. It has no mind to speak of and no court to serve. The Sylvan think it is what a pool becomes when it drinks a broken bargain.

The trouble with it is not killing it. The trouble is what happens after. A thing that is only a mouth does not die as other creatures die. It comes apart: three big pieces, four middling, two small, nine mouths where there was one, each a little weaker and every one still hungry. The Ardee children call it the Maw that won't stay dead, and dare each other to throw stones into its pool. The wise ones throw them from very far away.

The children are not wrong about the running.

The Ardee grandmothers, asked about it, tell the tale of the Dagda's porridge instead, which children like better. Before the second battle of Mag Tuired the Dagda went to the Fomorians' camp to ask for a truce, and the Fomorians, who knew how he loved porridge, made a mockery of him. They boiled eighty measures of new milk with meal and fat and whole goats and sheep and swine, poured it into a pit in the ground, and told him he would die if he left any. The Dagda took up his ladle, which was big enough for a man and a woman to lie in, and ate it all, and scraped the gravel at the bottom with his finger, and lay down and slept.

The grandmothers end the tale there, on the scraped pit and the sleeping god: a great appetite done well, by a mouth that knew when it had finished. The Green Maw is the other kind. It does not know when it has finished and it does not know when it is dead, and so each of its nine pieces goes on eating as if it were the whole. The Ardee children know the porridge tale by heart, and they sing the Dagda's meal at the edge of the pool, verse by verse, while they work up the nerve to throw.
legend: Killing it is the first half. When it dies it splits into nine pieces of three sizes: AoE them down, biggest first, and keep the healers clear of the splash. Have mana left for the second half, because that is where most bands lose it. Kill it, then kill nine more: AoE the pieces biggest first and keep mana for the second half. Superstition: never throw a stone into its pool unless you can outrun nine mouths. Old hands count the pieces aloud as they die, all nine, because one always hides in the reeds. Bards of Ardee sing a counting song about it.

loremasterTopic.text: A mouth grown in a pool of the Cursed Forest. It does not die so much as come apart into smaller mouths.

bookPage: From Derbáil of Ardee's list: the children of Ardee have a game, grandmother said, called Maw. You throw a stone into the green pool at the edge of the Cursed Forest from as far away as you can, and then you run. The one who throws from nearest wins, if they win. Grandmother forbade it, and so did her mother. It is still played. The realm's warriors say the thing in the pool comes apart when it dies, into nine smaller mouths, each still hungry. The children say they know. That is the point of running, and of throwing from far away.
